definition: Obstreperous means noisy and difficult to control.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word obstreperous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know obstreperous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The obstreperous freshman section drummed the bleachers through both anthems and every whistle.
Fidgety stops far short of obstreperous — fidgeting is squirmy motion, not defiance of the room.
Rowdy stops short of obstreperous — a rowdy crowd is loud in fun, while an obstreperous one is loud against control.

Unruly means refusing to be governed — an unruly class ignores the teacher no matter what the rules say, and it can do so in sullen silence. Obstreperous is unruliness at full volume: the obstreperous drown out whoever is trying to restore order. Unruly can be quiet defiance; obstreperous never is.

Raucous describes the sound itself — harsh, grating, ear-filling noise, whatever its purpose. Obstreperous is about the noise's target: an obstreperous crowd aims its racket against whoever is trying to bring it to order. A raucous gull colony is merely deafening; an obstreperous classroom is deafening at its teacher.

The heart of this word is Latin strepere, 'to make a racket' — a wonderfully noisy verb that left no other descendants in everyday English. You may recognize the prefix ob- ('against') from words like object, but the racket in obstreperous is all its own; learn the word whole.
Obstreperous means noisy and difficult to control.

Halfway through the estate auction, the back row turned obstreperous—bidding by air horn, shouting over the auctioneer's patter, rattling the folding chairs—until the gavel came down and the lot was withdrawn entirely.
Obstreperous adds defiance to volume: a loud room is merely noisy, but an obstreperous one is noisy against whoever is trying to run it—it resists being brought to order.
Obstreperous suits crowds, children, and animals who are loud and fighting control — often with a raised eyebrow of humor.
Plain 'rowdy' covers cheerful noise; reserve obstreperous for noise aimed at whoever is trying to restore order.
